prompt: A company's CI pipeline pushes a container image to Amazon ECR on every commit. A single repository in one account holds images for twenty services, and tens of thousands of untagged images and old development images have accumulated, increasing storage costs every month. Development tags start with dev-. Release-tagged images that start with v must not be deleted because of audits. Only two infrastructure engineers are on the team, and they do not want to maintain a separate cleanup script. The cleanup rule should be applied once to the entire repository regardless of service, and deleted images do not need to be recoverable. Currently, cleanup is done manually and occasionally by using a crontab on the CI server. Which cleanup method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Write a script that runs in an AWS Lambda function on a schedule, lists the images, selects the old images, and deletes them directly. Run the function by using Amazon EventBridge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delete and re-create the repository, and then push only the release images again from another repository to remove all unnecessary images.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an ECR lifecycle policy that expires untagged images after a set period and expires images with the development prefix tag beyond a set count. Exclude images with the v prefix from the rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable tag immutability on the repository so that the same tag cannot be overwritten, which causes old images to be cleaned up automatically.

explanation: A lifecycle policy is a managed ECR feature that automatically expires images according to rules, so there is no code or scheduler to operate, and a tag prefix condition can protect the release images. A Lambda deletion script does the same job, but you have to build and maintain it yourself. Re-creating the repository carries the risk and effort of moving the release images and also requires changing pipeline references. Tag immutability only prevents overwriting; it does not delete images.

prompt: A company deploys a web application by using an AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployment to an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group (12 instances) behind an Application Load Balancer. Deployments happen several times a day, including during business hours, and no staff are on call overnight. After the new version is installed, the deployment must check that the /health endpoint returns 200. If the check fails, the deployment must roll back to the last successful version without human intervention. The health check must be at the application level, not a port response, and the company wants to keep the existing deployment group configuration. Currently, deployments proceed one instance at a time and take less than 15 minutes. Changing the entire deployment process to a new tool is difficult given the schedule. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a health check script in the ValidateService hook and enable automatic rollback on failure for the deployment group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Put a health check script in the BeforeInstall hook of the AppSpec file and, if it fails, skip the install step so that the existing version is kept.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Connect only Amazon SNS notifications to the deployment group, without a CloudWatch alarm, and have an engineer manually redeploy the previous revision when the notification is received.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put a health check script in the ApplicationStop hook of the AppSpec file and, if there is no response, run the install script of the previous revision.

explanation: ValidateService is a hook that runs after installation and service start are complete, so it is the right place to check the state of the new version. If the script fails, the deployment fails, and automatic rollback redeploys the last successful revision. BeforeInstall runs before the new version is installed, so there is nothing to check yet. Manually redeploying after an SNS notification requires human intervention, which conflicts with the requirement. ApplicationStop is the step that stops the existing version and is not meant for validating the new version.

prompt: An AWS Lambda function at a fintech company reads a SecureString parameter from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store by using GetParameter (with WithDecryption set to true) to obtain a database connection string. The parameter is encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key in the same account, and other workloads also use this key. The key policy is set to allow delegation of permissions to IAM policies in the account. The function only reads the value, and the security team requires giving the execution role only the least privilege. The function code calls the parameter by a fixed name, and the parameter is in one location. The company has a single account, and the VPC endpoint configuration is already complete, so networking does not need to be considered. Which TWO least-privilege permissions should be granted to the function's execution role? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a statement to the execution role's policy that allows ssm:GetParameter on the ARN of the parameter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows kms:Encrypt on the customer managed key so that the function can re-encrypt the value it reads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a statement to the execution role's policy that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that was used for encryption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a statement that allows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on all secrets in the account so that the function can read values broadly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add a statement that allows ssm:PutParameter on the entire parameter path so that the function can read and update the value.

explanation: To read and decrypt a SecureString, both the ssm:GetParameter permission to read the parameter and the kms:Decrypt permission to decrypt the value are required. PutParameter is an unnecessary write permission for a function that only reads. kms:Encrypt is needed when storing a value, not when reading it. Secrets Manager permissions are for secrets in a different service, so they are unrelated to retrieving a Parameter Store parameter, and their scope is also too broad.

prompt: A logistics company's inventory service stores inventory items in an Amazon DynamoDB table. During peak season, inventory changes are frequent. When two AWS Lambda functions that read an item, change the quantity, and save it run concurrently on the same item, the last write overwrites the earlier change, quantities are lost, and customers complain. The team does not want to introduce a new lock table or lock service and does not want to change the table structure significantly. Because call frequency is high, retry logic is acceptable, but a design that significantly increases user response latency must be avoided. The table is in on-demand mode, and each item is smaller than 1 KB. Which method safely detects concurrent modifications with the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change reads to ConsistentRead, calculate the quantity after reading the latest quantity, and overwrite the same item with PutItem to reduce the gap between the read and the write.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have each function send an unconditional Put for the same item inside TransactWriteItems so that the two writes are processed serially.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a version attribute to the item, write by using an UpdateItem condition expression only when the version matches the version that was read, increment the version, and re-read and retry on failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collect the inventory change requests with DynamoDB Streams, have a single Lambda function apply them in order, and remove the original write path.

explanation: The correct answer is optimistic locking by using a version attribute and a conditional UpdateItem. If another write has changed the version since the read, the condition fails, so a lost update is detected, and only the failing side needs to re-read and retry, so no separate lock infrastructure is required. A strongly consistent read only guarantees the latest value at the moment of the read and does not prevent another write from slipping in between the read and the write. Putting an unconditional Put in a transaction does not change the fact that the last write wins. Streams are a record of changes made after a write, so they cannot remove the write path, and this approach significantly changes the structure.

prompt: A resize AWS Lambda function in an image processing service is configured with 512 MB of memory. It is invoked tens of thousands of times a day, so even small cost differences add up. The average run time is 8 seconds, and the function uses almost 100% of the CPU. Max Memory Used in the REPORT log is 180 MB. Users complain that processing delays are long, and the operations team wants to reduce the delay while minimizing any increase in monthly cost. The code is already optimized with no bottlenecks and will not be modified. The function runs outside a VPC, concurrency is sufficient, and the cold start time is negligible compared with the total of 8 seconds. Requests invoke the function asynchronously through Amazon S3 events. Which is the MOST cost-effective way to determine the memory setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because actual usage is 180 MB, lower the memory to 256 MB to reduce the GB-second price, and ignore any change in run time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency to create execution environments in advance so that the 8-second processing time becomes shorter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use AWS Lambda Power Tuning to measure run time and cost for each memory setting, and choose the setting with the lowest cost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the function timeout so that processing is not cut off midway, assume this reduces processing time, and leave the memory as is.

explanation: The correct answer is to use Lambda Power Tuning to measure run time and cost for each memory setting and choose from the results. Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, so for a CPU-bound function, increasing memory can significantly reduce run time, and the cost can stay the same or even drop. Power Tuning is the tool that confirms this by measurement. Lowering memory also reduces CPU, making the function slower and conflicting with the latency requirement. Provisioned concurrency is meant to mitigate cold starts and has no effect on the processing time itself. Increasing the timeout has nothing to do with processing speed.

prompt: The task definition of an Amazon ECS Fargate service specifies an AWS Secrets Manager secret in the secrets field so that it is injected as a container environment variable. After a new deployment, the task fails to start and a permission error occurs when retrieving the secret. The application code calls only Amazon S3, and that permission already exists in the task role. The secret value must be injected as an environment variable when the container starts, and the security team does not allow excessive permissions. The service is scheduled to launch next week, so the schedule is tight, and other services in the same cluster are already working normally. The secret is in the same account and the same Region and is not encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Which is the MOST appropriate solution that uses least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret to the task role so that the container can read the secret when it starts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the task execution role to resolve all permission errors, including secret retrieval, at once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the Principal in the secret's resource-based policy to a wildcard so that all principals in the account can retrieve the value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret on the task execution role, and also add kms:Decrypt if necessary.

explanation: Values injected through the secrets field are retrieved by the ECS agent by using the task execution role before the container starts, so granting GetSecretValue (and kms:Decrypt if needed) for the secret to the execution role is enough. The task role is the role used by the application code inside the container, so it is not used for injection at the startup stage. An administrator policy breaks the principle of least privilege, and a wildcard Principal exposes the secret far too broadly.

prompt: At a company, the network team manages a VPC stack with AWS CloudFormation, and several application teams must each reference the subnet IDs of that VPC from their own stacks. All stacks are in the same account and Region and have different lifecycles. The subnet IDs rarely change after deployment, but each team has a different deployment schedule, so a change to one stack must not have to wait for the deployment of another stack. Stack changes happen a few times a month and are deployed automatically in a CI pipeline, and the teams do not want to operate any additional services. The subnet IDs in the VPC stack will be shared between stacks going forward. Which method avoids hardcoding the subnet IDs in templates and has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restructure all application stacks as nested stacks with the VPC stack as the parent, and have the parent pass the subnet IDs as parameters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document a procedure in which the application teams look up the subnet IDs in the console on every deployment and enter them directly as template parameters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export the subnet IDs from the Outputs of the VPC stack and import them in the application stacks by using Fn::ImportValue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put a custom resource in each application stack so that a Lambda function finds the IDs with EC2 DescribeSubnets at deployment time and returns them.

explanation: Export and Fn::ImportValue let stacks in the same Region and account reference output values directly, so no hardcoding or manual entry is needed. Nested stacks are a structure in which the parent and children share a single lifecycle, so they do not fit a situation where teams and lifecycles differ. Manual entry is error-prone and has a high operational burden. A custom resource requires creating and maintaining Lambda code, which is excessive for a simple reference.

prompt: An AWS CloudFormation stack includes an Amazon EBS volume (AWS::EC2::Volume) that holds data. This volume is managed only by this stack and is not referenced by other stacks, and stack deletion permissions are open to many operators. Recently, a stack in a development environment was deleted by operator mistake, so the data at the time of deletion must be recoverable. However, to reduce costs, the company does not want to keep the volume itself indefinitely, and normal stack deletion must not be blocked. The volume totals 500 GiB, the recovery requirement is for the data as of just before the stack deletion, and a recovery time of up to several hours is acceptable. Snapshot storage costs are much lower than the cost of keeping the volume. Which method requires the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify DeletionPolicy Snapshot on the volume so that a snapshot is created before the stack is deleted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify DeletionPolicy Retain on the volume resource so that the volume remains as is even if the stack is deleted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable termination protection on the stack so that deletion requests fail until an administrator disables it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leave the deletion policy at its default and separately configure an Amazon EventBridge schedule rule so that a Lambda function creates volume snapshots every week.

explanation: If DeletionPolicy is set to Snapshot, CloudFormation creates a snapshot of the volume when the stack is deleted and then deletes the volume, so the data at the time of deletion is preserved and the volume cost goes away. Retain leaves the volume in place, so costs continue and the volume moves outside the stack's management. Termination protection blocks deletion itself, which conflicts with the conditions. Periodic snapshots preserve data only up to the time of the last run, not the time of deletion, and they also require separate operation.

prompt: Several internal payment services running on Amazon ECS call an Amazon API Gateway REST API in the same account. The callers are AWS workloads, not end users, and the team does not want to operate a new token issuing server or user directory. The call volume is not high, but the APIs that each service can call must differ, and the team does not want to increase the work of distributing and rotating credentials to each service. All calls are made from ECS tasks in the same VPC, and each service already has its own task role. The API has a Regional endpoint, and the services are written with the AWS SDK. Which authorization method controls permissions per caller and has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create dedicated service users in an Amazon Cognito user pool, attach a Cognito authorizer, and have the services call by using the tokens they receive when they sign in.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Lambda token authorizer and implement it yourself so that it validates a secret string shared by the services and sent in a header.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the method to AWS_IAM authorization, allow execute-api:Invoke on the task roles, and use SigV4 signing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue API keys through a usage plan, distribute them to each service, and turn on only the API key required setting on the method to identify callers.

explanation: IAM authorization verifies SigV4 signatures with the caller's IAM credentials, so no separate authentication server is needed, and the task role policies can divide the call permissions per service. The Cognito user pool approach requires operating a user directory for services and token refresh. A Lambda authorizer that validates a shared secret means you take on the code and secret rotation yourself. API keys are for usage control and are not designed to be used as an authorization or strong authentication mechanism.

prompt: In an order processing system, an AWS Lambda function that processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue opens connections to an Amazon RDS database. When events surge and the queue builds up, the concurrent executions of this function rise into the hundreds, exceed the database's maximum of 100 connections, and cause connection errors. Scaling up the database will be reviewed next quarter, and until then the team wants to control this on the function side first. The change must not affect other functions in the same account, and the team wants to cap the concurrent executions of this function at no additional charge. Queue messages may be delayed but must not be lost, and the queue's visibility timeout and retry configuration are already set appropriately. This function is also invoked directly through an API in addition to SQS, so a cap on the concurrent executions of the entire function is needed regardless of the invocation path. The team wants to solve this through configuration only, without code changes. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set provisioned concurrency of 100 on this function to reserve 100 pre-initialized execution environments so that no more than that are created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set reserved concurrency of 100 or less on this function to cap the concurrent executions of that function and separate it from the concurrency pool of other functions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the account-wide concurrent execution quota to 100 so that the concurrent executions of all functions stay within the database connection limit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shorten the function timeout to reduce connection hold time, hoping the connection count does not exceed the limit even as concurrent executions increase.

explanation: The correct answer is to set reserved concurrency on this function. Reserved concurrency limits the maximum concurrent executions of the function to prevent downstream resources such as a database from being overloaded, separates the pool from other functions, and has no additional charge. Provisioned concurrency sets the number of pre-initialized environments, is meant to mitigate cold starts, incurs charges, and does not prevent scaling beyond that number. The account quota is a service quota, is not something to lower for this purpose, and affects all functions. Shortening the timeout does not guarantee a cap on concurrent executions. For reference, the maximum concurrency setting on the SQS event source mapping also limits concurrent invocations per queue at no additional charge, but it applies only to invocations coming from that event source and cannot block direct invocations. This question requires a function-wide cap regardless of the invocation path, so reserved concurrency is correct. The two settings are independent, so when they are used together, the mapping's maximum concurrency should be set to no more than the reserved concurrency so that messages are not throttled.

prompt: A fintech app must encrypt the Korean resident registration number attribute of an Amazon DynamoDB item before storing it, so that plaintext is not exposed to the DynamoDB service or to principals that have table read permissions. Other attributes are used as query conditions, so they must remain plaintext, and the company wants to manage the key in AWS KMS. Regulations require that decryption of this attribute be auditable through AWS CloudTrail. The application is written in Java, and the development team has three people who do not want to implement the encryption logic themselves. Key usage records must be kept by using the default AWS auditing mechanism, without building a separate service. The table has tens of millions of items, and reads are mostly primary key lookups. Which method meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the AWS Database Encryption SDK to specify that only that attribute is encrypted on the client side, and use a KMS keyring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change encryption at rest for the table to a customer managed KMS key so that all attributes are encrypted with that key inside DynamoDB.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enforce TLS on connections to DynamoDB and use a VPC gateway endpoint policy so that only allowed roles can access the table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Block access to the resident registration number attribute by using the IAM condition key dynamodb:Attributes, and restrict all callers to reading only hash values.

explanation: The Database Encryption SDK provides attribute-level client-side encryption, so only the specified attribute is stored as ciphertext and the others can stay plaintext, and plaintext is not visible to the service or to principals with read permissions. Server-side encryption returns the decrypted value to callers that have permissions, so it does not meet the requirement. TLS and endpoint policies only control the transport and access path and do not hide the stored value itself. Restricting attribute access so that only hashes are read differs from the requirement to store the original value in a protected form.

prompt: An online store's order history screen has become slow, and the team is reviewing the Amazon DynamoDB table design. Each customer can accumulate up to several thousand orders, and the screen shows each customer's orders from most recent first. Customers must also be able to look up orders for a specific period (for example, from January 1 to March 31). Queries should use only Query, not Scan, and the team wants to avoid increased read costs from reading many items and discarding them with filters. Writes must not concentrate on a particular date. There are hundreds of thousands of customers, and a single customer does not place many orders per day. Each screen shows the 20 most recent orders. Which design is MOST appropriate when the problem is solved by primary key design alone, without adding secondary indexes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the order date as the partition key and the customer ID as the sort key, and for per-customer lookups, Query all partitions for the relevant dates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use only the order ID as the partition key, store the customer ID and date as regular attributes, and filter with a FilterExpression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the customer ID as the partition key and a value combining the date and the order ID as the sort key, and query by using a BETWEEN key condition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use only the customer ID as the partition key, store the date as a regular attribute, and sort the results of a per-customer Query in the application.

explanation: The correct answer is a design with the customer ID as the partition key and a value combining the date and the order ID as the sort key. A customer's orders sit in a single item collection sorted by date, so a sort key condition such as BETWEEN reads only the period needed, and ScanIndexForward=false returns the most recent orders first. Using the order date as the partition key concentrates writes on particular dates and scatters per-customer lookups across multiple partitions. A key of the order ID alone requires a Scan for per-customer lookups. Storing the date only as an attribute means reading all of a customer's orders and then filtering or sorting, which increases read cost.

prompt: A mobile app uploads files directly to Amazon S3 without going through a server. An AWS Lambda function (using its execution role) creates a presigned PUT URL for uploads with a validity period of 7 days and passes it to the app. Uploads succeed right after the URL is issued, but after a few hours they fail with an ExpiredToken error, according to inquiries. Bucket permissions and CORS are correct, and users often take photos and upload them later. The app is native, and the team wants to make server-side changes in only one place, the Lambda function. The target object key is a path separated by user ID, and for security reasons the URL should be valid only as long as necessary. What is the cause, and what is the MOST appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The signature expiration condition in the S3 bucket policy must be relaxed, so add a condition that allows s3:signatureAge and leave the URL validity period as is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The URL also expires when the role's temporary credentials expire, so shorten the URL validity period to fit within the credential lifetime and issue a new URL just before the upload.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The IAM role lacks the s3:PutObject permission, so add write permissions on the entire target bucket to the execution role's policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The PUT method is missing from the bucket CORS configuration, so add PUT to AllowedMethods to allow browser uploads.

explanation: The correct answer is to understand the relationship between the temporary credential lifetime and the URL validity period, and to issue a new URL just before the upload. According to the official documentation, a presigned URL created with temporary credentials becomes invalid at whichever comes first: the specified validity period or the time the credentials expire. If the URL is signed with role credentials, the URL also expires when the role session ends, even if 7 days is specified (7 days is the maximum possible with IAM user credentials and SigV4). Because the upload succeeded right after issuance, insufficient permissions are not the cause. A missing CORS setting would block the request from the start in a browser and does not explain signature expiry. The signatureAge condition is meant to reject old signatures, so it is not something that relaxes anything, and it does not fix credential expiry.

prompt: An IAM role for a development team has an identity-based policy that allows s3:*, and the same role has a permissions boundary set with a policy that allows only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. The bucket has no bucket policy, and the organization's SCPs do not block Amazon S3. The security team has formally approved uploads for this role, but developers' PutObject calls are blocked with AccessDenied. The role is shared by several developers, and its other permissions must be kept as they are now. The boundary policy is not attached to any other role and is dedicated to this role, and an IAM administrator can apply changes immediately. Which method resolves the problem with the SMALLEST change scope?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Explicitly add another statement that allows s3:PutObject to the role's identity-based policy to make the upload permission clear, and update the policy version.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows s3:PutObject to the permissions boundary policy so that uploads are included in the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include an allow for s3:PutObject in the session policy passed when assuming the role to temporarily expand permissions beyond the boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the role in addition to allow all actions, including those for Amazon S3.

explanation: A permissions boundary is the maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant, so the effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy. Adding PutObject to the boundary creates an intersection with the identity policy that already allows s3:*, and uploads open up. Writing the same allow again in the identity policy does not change the situation, because it is already allowed and is blocked by the boundary. A session policy can only reduce permissions and cannot widen them beyond the boundary. Attaching an administrator policy does not solve it either, because the boundary still acts as the upper limit.

prompt: An online shopping company is building an order workflow with AWS Step Functions that runs payment approval, inventory deduction, and shipping request in order across different services. For high-value orders, the workflow waits up to 3 days for approval from a person by using a callback token, and non-idempotent tasks such as payment must run exactly once. The execution history must be kept as audit material so that responsibility can be traced when failures occur, and the company handles thousands of orders per day. The team does not want to operate a workflow engine itself. The approvers for high-value orders are integrated by pressing a button in an internal approval tool, which returns the token. The entire processing of a single order takes from a few minutes to up to 3 days. Which workflow type is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Express asynchronous workflow. It is advantageous for high-volume processing, and execution status is checked in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a Standard workflow. It supports executions of up to 1 year, an exactly-once execution model, and waiting for a callback token.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Connect an Express synchronous workflow to Amazon API Gateway to receive the result in the call response, and also wait for the approval step in the same execution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Implement a chain in which a Lambda function directly invokes the next Lambda function, and handle the approval wait by repeated polling inside the function.

explanation: The correct answer is a Standard workflow. Standard workflows run for up to 1 year and use an exactly-once execution model, which suits non-idempotent tasks such as payment, and they support the callback (.waitForTaskToken) pattern and execution history lookup. Express workflows run for up to 5 minutes, asynchronous ones use at-least-once execution, and they do not support the callback pattern, so they violate both the 3-day approval wait and the run-only-once requirement. A Lambda chain with polling cannot wait 3 days inside a function that has a maximum run time of 15 minutes, and you would have to implement state management and error handling yourself, which is a heavy operational burden.

prompt: The buildspec of an AWS CodeBuild project builds an image with docker build and then pushes it to Amazon ECR. The project uses a Linux container environment, the source is in AWS CodeCommit, and the ECR repository has already been created in the same account and Region. The build currently fails with an error that it cannot connect to the Docker daemon, and it is expected that even after this error is fixed, a permission error will occur in the later push step. The team wants to fix only the CodeBuild settings without moving the build environment to a new service. Under security policy, the build environment image is the AWS managed Ubuntu standard image as is, and the ECR login is handled in the pre_build phase of the buildspec. Which TWO actions are needed to resolve the problem? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the source provider to Amazon S3 so that the buildspec can read the Docker context from the local file system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add the ecs:UpdateService permission to the CodeBuild service role so that the pushed image can be applied to the service immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the build environment image to a Windows Server image to use an environment in which the Docker daemon runs by default.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable privileged mode in the project environment so that the Docker daemon can run inside the build container.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Allow the CodeBuild service role ECR push permissions such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, image layer upload, and PutImage.

explanation: To build a Docker image inside CodeBuild, privileged mode must be turned on in the environment, and to push to ECR, the service role must have the authorization token, layer upload, and PutImage permissions. Switching to a Windows image is not a solution to the daemon connection problem. ecs:UpdateService is a permission needed in the deployment stage and is unrelated to pushing images. The source provider has nothing to do with Docker daemon access or ECR permissions.

prompt: A startup's mobile backend uses an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda proxy integration. After deploying a new endpoint, clients receive a 502 Bad Gateway response with Malformed Lambda proxy response. The Lambda logs show a normal completion with no errors, and the function returns a dictionary in the form {"message":"ok","items":[1,2,3]} as is. Other endpoints of the same API work normally, and there are no timeout-related logs. The frontend team expects a JSON body and must also receive CORS values in the response headers. The backend is written in Python. Which fix is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the function timeout beyond the API Gateway integration timeout so that the response is not cut off by delays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the handler return format so that the response is returned in a structure of statusCode, headers, and a string body.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add permission for the API Gateway service principal to invoke the function to the Lambda function's resource-based policy so that the invocation is not denied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on a cache cluster on the stage so that API Gateway returns a cached response even if the function's response format is wrong.

explanation: The correct answer is to change the handler to return a statusCode, headers, and body (string) format. In a Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway requires the function to respond in a defined JSON format, and it returns 502 Bad Gateway for any other format. The function being recorded as a normal completion is consistent with this explanation. A timeout is a setting for solving delay problems and is unrelated to a format error. If invocation permission were missing, the function itself would not be invoked and no normal completion would appear in the logs. A cache is meaningful only when there is a response with the correct format and cannot hide a format error.

prompt: A team that runs the post-payment stages serverlessly has an order processing AWS Lambda function that reads messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue with a batch size of 10. Daily volume is high, so reducing the batch size would significantly increase invocation costs. Currently, if even one message in a batch fails to process, the function throws an exception, and the remaining 9 messages also reappear in the queue and are processed twice, and some messages have already been processed twice. The function code can be modified. Processing takes about 1 second per message, and the function timeout is 30 seconds. Most failures are caused by transient external API errors, and a retry succeeds. Which is the MOST appropriate method to retry only the failed messages while keeping a batch size of 10 and making minimal changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the batch size to 1 so that the function is invoked separately for each message, and also increase the function concurrency limit to handle the increased number of invocations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping, and have the handler return only the messageId values of the failed messages as batchItemFailures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the visibility timeout of the source queue to 0 seconds so that only the failed messages become visible again immediately and the remaining messages are deleted as is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify an SQS standard queue as the DLQ in the Lambda function configuration so that the entire batch in which a failure occurred is stored in a separate queue and an operator reprocesses it later.

explanation: The correct answer is to set ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return only the failed messageId values as batchItemFailures. This deletes the successful messages from the queue and makes only the failed messages visible again, so the batch size of 10 is kept while duplicate processing is prevented. Reducing the batch size to 1 breaks the condition of the question (keep a batch size of 10) and only increases the number of invocations and the cost. Setting the visibility timeout to 0 seconds does not change the behavior of returning the entire batch that ended in an exception and makes the same messages be received repeatedly right away. A function-level DLQ is for asynchronous invocations; for an SQS event source, the DLQ must be placed on the queue side, and in either case the whole batch is stored, so it does not prevent reprocessing of successful messages.

prompt: A mobile game service queries a global secondary index (GSI) keyed on playerId right after saving a score to the Amazon DynamoDB base table, but the score just written is sometimes missing from the results. When the team turns on ConsistentRead to fix this, a ValidationException occurs. The results screen shown right after score submission must always show the latest score, and the overall ranking list screen can be a few seconds late. The table is in on-demand mode, and the team does not want to migrate data to a new table. The GSI has playerId as the partition key and is sorted by score, and the screen right after submission already knows the primary key of the item that was just saved. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For the screen right after submission, call GetItem on the base table by using the primary key and ConsistentRead, and use the GSI only for the list that tolerates delay.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the read capacity units of the global secondary index so that the index catches up with changes to the base table more quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a DAX cluster in front of the global secondary index to get index query results back from the cache consistently.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the projection of the global secondary index to ALL so that all attributes are in the index and the base table does not need to be read separately.

explanation: The correct answer is to query the base table by primary key with a strongly consistent read on the screen right after submission, and to use the GSI only for lists that tolerate delay. Reads from GSIs and streams support only eventual consistency and do not support strongly consistent reads, which causes the ValidationException; only the base table and LSIs support strongly consistent reads. Increasing read capacity does not change the consistency model. DAX is a cache layer and cannot make the guarantee of the latest value any stronger. Changing the projection to ALL only reduces table lookups; the index data is still eventually consistent.

prompt: A cost alarm goes off at 2 a.m. because the number of AWS Lambda invocations suddenly spikes. The cause is a recursive structure in which the function sends its processing results to an Amazon SQS queue, and that queue invokes the same function as an event source. Reviewing and deploying the fix is expected to take several hours, and costs must be stopped in the meantime. The function configuration and the messages in the queue must be preserved, and other functions in the same account must keep working normally. The function is connected through an SQS event source mapping, the code path that caused the recursion has already been identified, and only preparing the fix remains. The messages that have accumulated must be processed normally after the fix. Which is the MOST appropriate way to immediately stop only further executions of this function before the fix is deployed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to 0 so that all new invocations are throttled and not executed, and remove the limit after the fix.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delete the function so that no invocations occur, and when deploying the fix, create a new function with the same name and reconnect it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the function timeout to 1 second so that each invocation ends quickly, and wait for the recursion to die down naturally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the account-level Lambda concurrent execution quota on the Service Quotas screen to limit the execution of all functions.

explanation: The correct answer is to set reserved concurrency to 0. With reserved concurrency set to 0, all invocations of that function are throttled and not executed, so the cost increase can be stopped immediately before the code is fixed, the function configuration remains intact, and you only need to remove the setting after the fix. Deleting the function means you have to re-create the configuration and connection settings. Reducing the timeout does not stop the invocations themselves, so the recursion continues. Lowering the account quota stops other functions too, and service quotas are not meant to be lowered arbitrarily.

prompt: A compliance requirement states that all access to a specific Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted in transit and that HTTP requests must be denied. The bucket is shared by several teams, dozens of applications access it by using SDKs, and code deployment schedules differ by team, so the code of each application cannot be modified. SSE-S3 default encryption is already applied to the bucket. The audit is next month, and the security team wants to apply the control once, centrally, without coordinating with each team. Both uploading and downloading objects are done through existing IAM roles, and whether VPC endpoints are used differs by team. Which method meets this requirement with the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable SSE-S3 default encryption on the bucket so that all objects are encrypted at rest and transport is also protected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a condition that allows only HTTPS requests into each team's application IAM policy, ask the teams to deploy the policies, and check whether they have been applied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning so that objects written over unencrypted transport can be rolled back to a previous version.

explanation: If the bucket policy explicitly denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, no caller can access the bucket over HTTP, and no client code change is needed. SSE-S3 encrypts data at rest and does not enforce the transport channel. Putting a condition in each team's IAM policy requires changes and coordination for every team and cannot block principals that are missed. Versioning is only a recovery feature and does not prevent plaintext transport.

prompt: The operations team has been receiving the same failure alarm repeatedly for several hours. In an AWS Lambda function that uses an Amazon SQS standard queue as its event source, a particular message always causes an exception and keeps being received again. An SQS queue was specified as the DLQ in the function settings, but no messages accumulate in that queue. The problem message must be kept for later root cause analysis, and processing of normal messages must continue. About 50,000 messages a day arrive in the source queue, the problem messages are a small number of malformed messages, and the alarm is set in Amazon CloudWatch on the function's error count. Which is the MOST appropriate action to isolate the problem message after a set number of attempts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the on-failure destination of the event source mapping to an SQS queue and set the function's maximum retry attempts to 2 to configure the same isolation effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduce the message retention period of the source queue to 1 minute so that messages that could not be processed disappear from the queue on their own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the function-level DLQ target to an Amazon SNS standard topic so that failure events are delivered at the same time to a subscribed email address and queue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Connect a DLQ to the source queue with a redrive policy that specifies maxReceiveCount, so that a message received a set number of times is moved to the DLQ.

explanation: The correct answer is to connect a DLQ to the source queue with a redrive policy that has maxReceiveCount. When SQS is used as the event source, the DLQ must be configured on the queue itself, not on the Lambda function; a function-level DLQ applies only to asynchronous invocations, which is why the queue is empty now. The on-failure destination and maximum retry attempts are asynchronous invocation settings and are not an isolation mechanism for an SQS event source mapping. Reducing the retention period makes normal messages disappear along with the problem message, leaving no data to analyze. Changing the function-level DLQ to SNS does not change the situation, because it applies only to asynchronous invocations.

prompt: A fintech company's point transfer API processes, in a single Amazon DynamoDB table, a balance deduction for the sender (only when the balance is at least the amount), a balance increase for the recipient, and the addition of a history item. Because of financial regulations, all three operations must either all succeed or all fail, and intermediate states must not be visible externally. Even if the client resends the same request because of a network timeout, a double transfer must not occur. All items are in one table in the same Region, and the team does not want to add a separate coordination service. Traffic is at the level of hundreds of requests per second, and a single transfer touches three items. The app uses the AWS SDK directly, and the client sends a unique request ID with every request. Which implementation is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Send two Updates and one Put in a single BatchWriteItem call, and resend if UnprocessedItems appears in the response.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Put two conditional Updates and one Put in a single TransactWriteItems call, and resend with the same ClientRequestToken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Call the three operations in order with UpdateItem and PutItem, and if one fails midway, perform compensating calls that undo the operations that already succeeded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collect write results with DynamoDB Streams, and have a Lambda function correct the differences periodically if the balance totals do not match.

explanation: The correct answer is to put two conditional Updates and one Put in a single TransactWriteItems call and secure idempotency with ClientRequestToken. A transaction either fully succeeds or fully fails and can also use condition expressions, and if it is resent with the same token, it returns success without any change within the token validity time (10 minutes). BatchWriteItem as a whole is not atomic and cannot specify condition expressions. The compensating call approach exposes intermediate states externally, and the compensation itself can fail. Correcting after the fact with Streams means there are moments when the balance is wrong, so it does not meet the atomicity requirement.

prompt: A payment service runs as an Amazon ECS service on Fargate (desired task count of 4) and is connected to Application Load Balancer health checks. Deployments are done several times a day as rolling updates, and no one is on standby at night. The number of healthy tasks must not drop during a deployment, and if new tasks repeatedly fail to start, the service must return to the last healthy deployment without human intervention. A large change such as switching the deployment method to AWS CodeDeploy is difficult this quarter. The ECS service already uses the rolling update deployment controller, and task definition updates are made automatically in the CI pipeline. The cluster has sufficient Fargate capacity quota. Which configuration meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 50 and maximumPercent to 100, and enable the circuit breaker with the rollback option.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 100 and maximumPercent to 200, and enable the deployment circuit breaker with the rollback option.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set both minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent to 100, and if it fails, have an engineer manually roll back to the previous task definition in the console.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch the service to the CodeDeploy blue/green deployment controller and configure rollback with two target groups and a separate AppSpec file.

explanation: If the minimum healthy percent is set to 100 and the maximum percent is opened to 200, new tasks are started first and then the old tasks are reduced, so capacity is maintained, and the circuit breaker of the rolling deployment controller automatically rolls back to the last completed deployment when the failure threshold is exceeded. A minimum percent of 50 allows healthy tasks to drop to half during a deployment. If both are 100, there is no room to start additional new tasks, so the deployment does not progress. Switching to blue/green is a big change, and the requirements can be met within rolling updates.

prompt: In a SaaS company's Amazon API Gateway REST API, a Lambda authorizer (TOKEN type) validates the token and then returns a policy that allows only the ARN of the single method that was requested first. The result cache TTL is the default of 300 seconds, and the cache was turned on intentionally to reduce the number of authorizer invocations. However, when the same token is used to call a different path, a 403 is returned for a period of time even though the user is authorized. Per-user permissions themselves are being calculated correctly. The authorizer Lambda function queries the user database every time to determine permissions, so reducing the number of invocations is important for cost. Which solution is MOST appropriate while keeping the cache?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Widen the policy Resource to a wildcard for the entire stage path of the API so that the cached policy is also valid for other methods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the authorization result cache TTL to the maximum of 3600 seconds so that the policy for the same token is reused for longer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the authorizer type to REQUEST with only the Authorization header as the identity source and keep the TTL so that policies are generated anew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the memory of the authorizer Lambda function to shorten validation time, which also widens the scope of the policy for the first request.

explanation: The correct answer is to widen the policy Resource to the entire stage path so that the cached policy applies to other methods too. For the TOKEN type, the token header value is the cache key, so the same policy is reused during the TTL for the same token; if a policy that allows only a specific method ARN is cached, requests for other paths with the same token are denied because they are not covered by the policy. The official documentation also advises that when caching is on, the policy must fit all resources and methods of the API. Increasing the TTL only lengthens the time of denial. For the REQUEST type, the cache key is divided only when context variables such as the path are included in the identity source; if a single header is the only identity source, the same value uses the same cache, so this does not solve the problem. Function memory affects only validation speed and has nothing to do with the scope of the policy.

prompt: A SaaS company provides its API on a paid basis to three external B2B customers, and the allowed call volume differs by customer according to contract terms. A different request rate limit per second and a different monthly call quota must be applied to each customer, and a surge of calls from one customer must not block calls from other customers. The backend consists of AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB, and the number of customers will increase to ten next month. The development team wants to implement this by using only Amazon API Gateway settings, without changing the backend code. Each customer can be identified by a key passed in a header, and authentication is already handled by a separate authorizer. There is a single stage, prod. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the stage's default method throttling values so that all customers share the same per-second limit, and return 429 when a surge occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Issue an API key for each customer, create usage plans with different rate, burst, and quota values, and associate them with the keys and the stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the backend Lambda function's reserved concurrency to the value divided by the number of customers so that throughput is split evenly among customers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Implement the backend Lambda function to count the calls per customer with a DynamoDB counter and to generate and return a 429 response itself when the limit is exceeded.

explanation: The correct answer is a per-customer API key and usage plan. A usage plan uses an API key as a client identifier and sets rate, burst, and quota per key, so per-customer limits can be divided by configuration alone. Default stage throttling does not distinguish customers and applies the same limit, so one customer's surge affects other customers. Function reserved concurrency is a per-function cap and cannot express customer distinctions or a monthly quota. Implementing a counter yourself violates the constraint of not changing the backend code and also carries a heavy operational burden.

prompt: A Python AWS Lambda function in a news app backend is seeing both cost and response time rise as traffic grows. A performance review revealed a bottleneck: the function creates a new boto3 DynamoDB client inside the handler on every invocation. Of the 120 ms average run time, about 60 ms is spent creating the client and establishing the connection. The function is invoked dozens of times per second, and the cold start rate is low. Given the schedule, the development team allows only a fix of one or two lines and no structural changes. The function runs outside a VPC, there are no problems with IAM permissions or the runtime version, and the same function creates a few other AWS clients as well. Which method reduces run time MOST effectively with minimal code changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Move the client creation to the initialization phase outside the handler so that subsequent invocations reuse the same client.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double the function memory to increase the CPU used for client creation, and leave the handler code as is to reduce the scope of change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency to create execution environments in advance so that the client creation time disappears on every invocation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep creating the client inside the handler but reduce the SDK's maximum attempts to lower the cost of connection attempts.

explanation: The correct answer is to create the client in the initialization phase outside the handler and reuse it. Lambda reuses execution environments, so SDK clients and connections created in the initialization phase are used as is in subsequent invocations, and the creation cost incurred on every invocation disappears. Increasing memory increases CPU and may reduce the time somewhat, but it raises cost and repeats the same work fundamentally. Provisioned concurrency is for cold starts, and the code that creates the client each time the handler is invoked still runs. Maximum attempts is a retry policy and is unrelated to creation cost.

prompt: A logistics company's order processing application runs on six Amazon EC2 instances and calls Amazon SQS and Amazon DynamoDB by using IAM user access keys stored in a configuration file. The burden of manually rotating the keys every quarter is large, and a security audit flagged the use of long-term credentials, so this must be improved by next month. The application uses the latest AWS SDK, and the instances are in the same account. Developer staff are limited, so the company wants to keep application code changes to a minimum. The instances are newly created when they are replaced by an Auto Scaling group, and the company has no separate in-house system for storing keys. The application runs only inside the instances. Which is the MOST appropriate way to eliminate the long-term keys?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Move the access keys to AWS Secrets Manager, configure automatic rotation with a rotation Lambda function, and have the application read the value at startup.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replace the access keys in the configuration file with values encrypted by AWS KMS, and have the application decrypt them at startup and pass them to the SDK client.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach an IAM role that has the required permissions through an instance profile, and delete the keys from the configuration file so that the SDK default credential chain uses temporary credentials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have the instance user data script call GetSessionToken with the IAM user keys, renew the credentials with cron before they expire, and write them to environment variables.

explanation: An IAM role attached through an instance profile automatically issues and renews temporary credentials through instance metadata, and the SDK's default credential provider chain finds and uses them without code changes. Keys moved to Secrets Manager or encrypted with KMS are still long-term IAM user keys, so the audit finding is not resolved and rotation operations remain. The GetSessionToken approach also requires long-term IAM user keys and creates a new operational burden in the form of a renewal script.

prompt: In an image sharing service, when an object is created in the images bucket, an AWS Lambda function creates a thumbnail and saves it to the same bucket. However, the bucket notification is configured for all ObjectCreated events, so saving a thumbnail invokes the function again, creating a recursion, and the number of invocations and costs surged. For now, the team stopped the function by setting reserved concurrency to 0. Now the structure must be fixed so that the same problem does not recur, and the original objects uploaded by users must be preserved as they are. Both changing the output location in the function code and changing the bucket notification configuration are possible, and the original objects that have already accumulated will not be touched. In addition to the cost alarm, the team wants to block the recursion fundamentally. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate to prevent recurrence? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the function timeout so that no subsequent invocation for the same object starts before thumbnail creation finishes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a prefix filter (for example, uploads/) to the bucket notification and save thumbnails under a different prefix (for example, thumbs/).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the function memory to lower the cost per invocation so that the total cost stays below the threshold even if recursion occurs, accepting the performance degradation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify an SQS queue as the function-level DLQ so that failure events from recursive invocations are stored in the queue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Save thumbnails to a separate output bucket that is different from the original bucket so that output writes do not trigger notifications on the input bucket.

explanation: The correct answers are to separate the output bucket and to apply a prefix filter on the notification that excludes the output path. The cause of the recursion is that the objects the function writes match the same notification conditions again, so the output must be excluded from the notification targets, and Lambda best practices also advise avoiding architectures in which a function invokes itself again. Increasing the timeout does not break the chain of invocations. Reducing memory only changes how fast cost grows and does not prevent recursion, while performance gets worse. A DLQ only stores failed events and does not block successful recursive invocations.

prompt: A daily report AWS Lambda function in an order management system reads OPEN items from an 8 GB Amazon DynamoDB table by using a Scan with ConsistentRead turned on and a FilterExpression (status = OPEN). OPEN items are only a tiny fraction of all items, yet a large amount of read capacity is consumed, and other requests that use the same table are throttled. The report results can be reflected a few seconds late, and the team does not want to change the table capacity mode. The report runs once a day, and the total number of items is tens of millions. The cost of adding an index is acceptable, but the table's existing key structure cannot be changed. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate to reduce read capacity consumption? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the Scan to a parallel Scan with a large TotalSegments to reduce the total read capacity units consumed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use ProjectionExpression to return only the needed attributes so that the size of the items read shrinks and read capacity decreases with it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a GSI that uses status as the partition key and Query that index instead of using Scan, so that only OPEN items are read.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because results may be a few seconds late, turn off ConsistentRead and switch to eventually consistent reads to halve the read cost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Make the FilterExpression condition stricter to reduce the number of items the server returns, which also reduces read capacity consumption.

explanation: The correct answers are to Query a GSI based on status and to switch to eventually consistent reads. A Scan reads the entire table and consumes capacity regardless of the filter, so a Query that narrows the range to read by using a key condition is efficient, and an eventually consistent read costs half of a strongly consistent read, and the requirement tolerates a few seconds of delay. A filter is applied after reading, so making the condition stricter does not reduce consumed capacity. A parallel Scan increases speed but raises capacity demand even more. ProjectionExpression only reduces the returned attributes, and read capacity is calculated based on the full size of the items read.

prompt: In a message processing system, ten Amazon EC2 workers run 24 hours a day and repeatedly call ReceiveMessage on an Amazon SQS standard queue with default settings. Cost analysis shows that most of the SQS request charges come from empty responses. The queue is empty most of the time, empty responses number in the millions per day, and request costs keep rising. However, messages must be processed as quickly as possible once they arrive, so an approach that significantly increases processing delay is not acceptable. Each receive call currently returns up to 10 messages, and workers delete them immediately after processing. Changing the queue type is meaningless because message ordering is not required. Which is the MOST appropriate way to reduce cost while still receiving messages as soon as possible after they arrive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the code so that a worker sleeps for 30 seconds after receiving an empty response and then calls again, to reduce the number of empty responses received.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the queue's visibility timeout to 12 hours so that a message stays hidden for a long time once it is received.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use long polling by setting WaitTimeSeconds to 20 seconds (or setting the queue attribute ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to 20).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the queue type from standard to FIFO so that responses are returned only in the order in which messages arrive.

explanation: The correct answer is to use long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds). With long polling, the server waits for a response until a message arrives, so empty responses and false empty responses decrease and request costs fall, and when a message arrives it is returned right away, so the delay is also short. Sleeping 30 seconds after an empty response reduces the number of calls but delays message receipt by that much. The visibility timeout is the time until a received message becomes visible again and has nothing to do with the number of empty responses. Switching to FIFO is an ordering feature and does not change the polling method.

prompt: A team created an AWS CodeDeploy deployment group for a new Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and deployed for the first time, but the deployment does not progress on the instances. The logs show that the agent cannot be found and an access denied error for the Amazon S3 revision. The service role and deployment group settings are correct. The instances run Amazon Linux, go out to the internet through NAT in a private subnet, and the revision is stored in an S3 bucket in the same account. The problem must be resolved without creating a new instance AMI. The deployment group identifies instances by Auto Scaling group name, and the instances already have the SSM Agent installed, so commands can be run through AWS Systems Manager if needed. Which TWO actions are needed to resolve the problem? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allow the s3:GetObject permission to read objects in the S3 bucket where the revision is stored on the role of the instance profile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Install the CodeDeploy agent on the instances by using launch template user data or Systems Manager, and keep it running.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a rule that allows inbound port 22 on the instance security group so that the CodeDeploy service can connect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open inbound port 443 to all IP addresses on the instance security group so that the CodeDeploy service pushes deployments to the agent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attach the CodeDeploy service role to the instances as an instance profile so that the instances download the revision with the service role permissions.

explanation: EC2 deployments require the CodeDeploy agent to be installed on the instances, and because the agent downloads the revision from S3 with the permissions of the instance profile role, read permission on that bucket is required. The service role is a role that the CodeDeploy service assumes, so it is not attached to instances. The agent works by polling CodeDeploy outbound over port 443, so opening inbound port 22 or 443 does not make deployments get pushed.

prompt: In a service that invokes an AWS Lambda function from Amazon DynamoDB Streams whenever order data changes to update a search index, IteratorAge keeps increasing. The service owner is concerned that the processing delay could turn into a data consistency problem. The function takes a long time per batch of records and processes only one batch at a time per shard. Changes to the same item must be processed in order, and the number of shards is determined by AWS, so it cannot be increased directly. The current batch size is 100, and the cause of the longer processing time is that responses from the external search service have become slow. The function already has sufficient memory and concurrency. Which is the MOST appropriate way to increase throughput while preserving order?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce the batch size to 1 so that processing time per invocation becomes shorter and processing speed increases as the number of invocations grows.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase ParallelizationFactor to raise the number of concurrent batches per shard, while records with the same partition key are still processed in order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the stream retention period to 7 days so that records do not expire even as IteratorAge grows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change StartingPosition to LATEST and re-create the mapping so that the accumulated records are skipped and reading starts from the newest records.

explanation: The correct answer is to increase ParallelizationFactor. This setting lets a single shard be processed with up to 10 concurrent batches, which raises throughput when IteratorAge is high, and records with the same partition key are grouped into the same concurrent batch and processed in order, and DynamoDB Streams guarantees ordering per item. Reducing the batch size to 1 could make serial per-shard processing even slower. The stream data retention period is fixed at 24 hours and cannot be increased by the user. Restarting with LATEST permanently loses the skipped records.

prompt: A sign-up API for a service expecting a large increase in concurrent requests because of a sign-up event saves a user item with PutItem to an Amazon DynamoDB table whose partition key is the email address. When two requests with the same email arrive almost simultaneously, there has been an incident in which the item saved first was overwritten. If the email already exists, the save must be rejected, but the team does not want to add read requests during the event period. The table structure will not be changed. Normally there is one request per user, but a double request can arrive because of a retry button. Response latency must stay in the single-digit milliseconds. Which implementation is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before saving, check whether the email exists with GetItem using ConsistentRead, and save with PutItem only when there is no result.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a global secondary index on the email attribute and Query that index before saving to check for a duplicate email first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receive INSERT events with DynamoDB Streams and, if there are two or more items with the same email, delete the item that was written later.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add an attribute_not_exists(email) condition expression to PutItem and respond with a duplicate error when ConditionalCheckFailedException occurs.

explanation: The correct answer is to add an attribute_not_exists(email) condition expression to PutItem and handle ConditionalCheckFailedException as a duplicate. Condition evaluation and the write happen in a single atomic request, so overwriting is prevented without any additional reads. Checking first with GetItem leaves a gap between the check and the write, so the same problem reproduces under concurrent requests, and it also incurs read costs. A global secondary index supports only eventual consistency and may miss an item that was just saved. Deleting after the fact with Streams cannot recover the data that was saved first and has already been overwritten.

prompt: In a file processing service, an AWS Lambda function is invoked asynchronously when a file is uploaded to Amazon S3. The operations team wants to analyze the causes of failures quickly. When the function still fails after two retries, the team wants to receive in Amazon SQS a record that includes not only the original event but also invocation result information such as the function error response and retry count, and analyze it. The function code uses a library shared by several teams, so the team wants to solve this by using configuration only, without modifying the code. The failure record must contain enough information to reprocess the failed event, and the queue has already been created as a standard SQS queue. The invoker is the S3 event notification. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify an SQS standard queue as the function-level DLQ so that the failed event and the entire error response returned by the function accumulate in the queue together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add try/catch to the function code and send the error information directly to SQS with the SDK's SendMessage whenever an exception occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the asynchronous invocation configuration, specify an SQS standard queue as the On failure destination so that the invocation record JSON is delivered to the queue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduce the maximum retry attempts of the asynchronous invocation to 0 and send the error logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to SQS with a subscription filter.

explanation: The correct answer is to specify an SQS standard queue as the On failure destination in the asynchronous invocation configuration. The destination record contains the request payload along with response information (such as the function error type and invocation count) as JSON. A DLQ delivers only the event content and does not include response details, so it does not meet the analysis requirement. Putting SendMessage in the code violates the constraint of not modifying the code and also cannot catch errors where the process terminates abnormally. Reducing retries to 0 and using a log subscription filter only removes the chance to retry and still does not deliver the invocation record itself.

prompt: A SAM template contains 20 AWS Lambda functions, and all of them include the same internal utility library of about 8 MB in each deployment package. The library is modified three or four times a month, and each time the 20 packages must be rebuilt and deployed, so the pipeline runs frequently and the burden is large. All functions use the same Python runtime and are in one account and one Region, and library loading must not increase cold start time. Both the total size and the per-function size of the deployment packages are within limits, so size limits are not a problem. The team builds and deploys with the SAM CLI and is familiar with using layers. Which is the MOST appropriate way to reduce duplication and simplify library updates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Encode the entire library in Base64, put it in the environment variable of each function, and have the function decode it at startup and unpack it into a temporary directory to use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Merge the 20 functions into a single function that is rewritten to branch by path, so that the library is included only once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Upload the library to Amazon S3 and have each function download it on every invocation, so that it is updated without code changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Separate the library into a Lambda layer and have each function reference a layer version; when updating, publish a new layer version and change the references.

explanation: A Lambda layer separates a common library from function code so that several functions share it, which reduces package size and duplication, and updates are simplified by publishing a new layer version and having the functions reference that version. Environment variables have a size limit, so they cannot hold 8 MB. Merging the functions into one increases coupling and mixes permissions and deployment units. Downloading from S3 on every invocation increases latency and cost and also requires code changes.

prompt: An AWS Lambda function in account B must read and decrypt Amazon S3 objects that are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key in account A. Under security policy, the key stays only in account A and is not replicated to account B or shared as key material. The Lambda execution role is in account B, and the S3 permissions to read the objects have already been granted. There are thousands of encrypted objects, so the company wants to avoid re-encrypting them. The two accounts belong to the same organization. Because S3 permissions for reading objects already exist, only the key usage permission needs to be resolved. The security team of account B does not allow creating a new key. Which TWO configurations are needed to meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a statement to the key policy of the account A key that allows account B (or the relevant role in account B) to use kms:Decrypt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a new KMS key with the same alias name in account B and configure Lambda to decrypt by using the alias.

choices.label: C
