choices.text: Add a statement that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the account A key to the IAM policy of the Lambda execution role in account B.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modify the key policy of the AWS managed key aws/s3 in account A to allow the root user of account B to decrypt, and also share the key alias setting with account B.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add the canonical user ID of account B to the ACL of the account A S3 bucket to delegate both object and key usage permissions.

explanation: To use a KMS key across accounts, the key policy in the account that owns the key must allow the external account, and the IAM policy in the external account must delegate that permission to the execution role; neither one alone is sufficient. AWS managed keys have key policies that users cannot modify, so they cannot be used as a sharing target. A key with the same alias created in account B is a different key, so it cannot decrypt ciphertext from account A. A bucket ACL concerns object access and does not grant permission to use a KMS key.

prompt: An e-commerce backend application invokes an AWS Lambda function synchronously with the AWS SDK. Every time traffic surges during promotion periods, TooManyRequestsException (HTTP 429) is returned and the Throttles metric in Amazon CloudWatch rises. The account has many functions for other services that share the concurrent execution quota, and because callers wait for user responses, some delay is acceptable but requests must not be lost. Traffic spikes occur briefly a few times a day, and average concurrent executions normally stay within the quota. The number of requests arriving during a promotion jumps to several times the normal level for a moment, and most of the function's run time is spent waiting for responses from an external payment API, so increasing memory barely reduces run time. The function produces the same result on every invocation, so retrying has no side effects. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate to reduce this error? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the function timeout to the maximum so that invocations wait until the end without being throttled even if they take a long time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify an SQS queue as the function-level DLQ so that requests from throttled synchronous invocations are stored in the queue and automatically processed again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use retries with exponential backoff and jitter on SDK calls so that temporarily throttled invocations are retried at staggered times.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the function memory to reduce the run time of each invocation, and leave the account quota and concurrency settings as they are.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Request an increase of the account concurrent execution quota in Service Quotas, and assign reserved concurrency to the critical function.

explanation: The correct answers are retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and an increase of the concurrent execution quota together with reserved concurrency for the critical function. When a synchronous invocation exceeds the concurrency limit, it is throttled with a 429, so the client's backoff retries smooth out the spike, and if the limit itself is insufficient, the quota is raised and reserved concurrency guarantees the critical function's share (reserved concurrency keeps other functions from using that share and has no additional charge). Increasing the timeout does not make over-limit invocations wait; they are rejected. A function-level DLQ is used for asynchronous invocation failures, so it does not store throttled synchronous requests. Increasing memory helps only if run time shrinks, given that concurrency is roughly requests per second multiplied by average run time; in this problem most of the time is spent waiting on an external API, so run time barely shrinks, and even if it did, it would not prevent exceeding the limit during an instantaneous surge or guarantee quota, and it only increases cost.

prompt: Developers on dozens of project teams must be able to start and stop only the Amazon EC2 instances that carry their own team's project tag. Developers use roles by assuming them through SSO, and the number of project teams keeps growing, so the company wants to eliminate the burden of modifying IAM policies every time a new project is created. Instances of other teams must not be operated, and the security team does not want the number of policy files to grow. The instances already carry a consistent project tag. Developers do not create instances for their own project; they only start and stop them, and the roles can pass team information as a session tag at SSO sign-in. Which permission model is the MOST scalable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an IAM policy and group for each project, list the ARNs of that project's instances as the Resource, and add team members to the group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: List the ARNs of all project instances in a single role shared by all developers, and update the policy every time a project is added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give developers full EC2 permissions and detect instances without a project tag after the fact with an AWS CloudTrail alarm and correct them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach the project tag to both the principal and the instances, and use a single policy that allows actions only when aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag match.

explanation: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) handles all projects with a single condition that compares the principal tag with the resource tag, so even when a new project is created, you only need to set the tags without changing the policy. Creating a policy and group for each project increases the number of managed items in line with the number of projects. Listing ARNs in a shared role causes policy size limits and update burden and also does not separate teams. Granting full permissions and detecting afterward does not block access in advance.

prompt: A document management SaaS encrypts per-customer data keys with a symmetric AWS KMS key. The security team wants decryption to always fail if one customer's ciphertext is submitted for decryption with another customer's context, and wants to identify which customer's data was being decrypted through AWS CloudTrail during audits. There are millions of decrypt calls per day and thousands of customers, so the company wants to avoid the operational overhead of increasing the number of keys per customer. The application code can be modified. Currently, a single data key encrypts all customers' data, and there is only one KMS key. Call latency must not increase. Which is the MOST appropriate method that meets both requirements without increasing the number of keys to manage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a separate KMS key for each customer, put the customer ID in the alias, encrypt and decrypt with that alias on each call, and manage a key policy for each customer separately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pass the customer ID as the encryption context in the Encrypt and GenerateDataKey calls, and require the same context at Decrypt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach the customer ID as a plaintext prefix to the stored ciphertext, and implement the application to compare the prefix before decryption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to an asymmetric KMS key, put the customer ID in the encryption context, and encrypt with the public key and decrypt with the private key.

explanation: The encryption context is additional authenticated data that is cryptographically bound to the ciphertext, so if the same context is not supplied at decryption, KMS refuses to decrypt, and the context values are also recorded in CloudTrail logs. Creating a key per customer greatly increases the number of keys to manage, which conflicts with the requirement. Comparing a plaintext prefix is not cryptographically bound to the ciphertext and depends on the application having no bugs. The encryption context is supported only for symmetric key operations, so an asymmetric key cannot meet this requirement.

prompt: An AWS Lambda function retrieves database credentials with GetSecretValue from AWS Secrets Manager on every invocation. The function runs dozens of concurrent executions all day long, latency increases when hundreds of invocations per second arrive, and API call cost and the risk of throttling also grow. The secret is rotated periodically under security policy, so its value must not be fixed permanently, and the new value must be reflected soon after rotation. The function is currently written in Python and runs inside a VPC, and the secret has automatic rotation configured in Secrets Manager in the same Region. Which is the MOST efficient way to improve this with minimal code changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Read the secret value at deployment time, copy it as plaintext into the Lambda environment variables, and redeploy the function configuration every time the secret is rotated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the secret as an encrypted file in an Amazon S3 bucket, have the function download it once at startup and keep it in /tmp, and keep using it without checking whether it has been rotated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include a credentials file in the function deployment package, and have the CI pipeline rebuild and redeploy the package on every rotation cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the Secrets Manager caching client (or the extension for Lambda) to cache the secret in execution environment memory and refresh it after it expires.

explanation: With the caching client or the Parameters and Secrets extension, the value is reused inside the execution environment, which reduces the number of calls and latency, and a new value is fetched after the cache TTL elapses, so a rotated secret is also reflected. Copying it into an environment variable requires redeployment on every rotation and exposes the value in plaintext. Downloading an S3 file only once means rotation is not reflected. Including credentials in the package leaves secrets in the code repository and artifacts, which is the least secure option.

prompt: The logs of an order settlement batch job that calls Amazon DynamoDB contain a mix of three errors. ProvisionedThroughputExceededException appears intermittently, ConditionalCheckFailedException appears occasionally, and ValidationException appears repeatedly for certain requests. The batch runs overnight for several hours, and some failures are acceptable, but the job must not stop because of transient errors or loop forever because of permanent errors. The batch code relies on the default retry behavior of the AWS SDK, and the condition failures were confirmed to occur when another worker updated the item first. Which design for the retry policy by error type is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave throughput exceeded errors to the SDK's exponential backoff retries, decide on condition failures by re-reading the item, and fix the request for validation errors without retrying.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retry all three errors with exponential backoff the same number of times, keeping the policy simple by not distinguishing between transient and permanent problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Do not retry throughput exceeded errors and record them as failures immediately, and repeat condition failures and validation errors with no wait until they succeed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retry validation errors with exponential backoff because they are transient problems, and discard throughput exceeded errors on the assumption that the request itself is wrong.

explanation: The correct answer is a design that leaves throughput exceeded errors to SDK retries, decides on condition failures after re-reading, and fixes the request for validation errors. Throttling is transient, so retrying with exponential backoff succeeds; a condition failure is the logical result of a false condition expression; and client errors such as ValidationException keep failing even if the same request is sent again, so they are not retry targets. Retrying all errors the same way wastes time and capacity on requests that will fail. Discarding throughput exceeded errors loses data because of a transient error, and retrying validation errors repeats the same failure.

prompt: A SaaS company's AWS CodePipeline has source, build, staging deployment, and production deployment stages. A release manager must approve immediately before the production deployment, and the approval request must be delivered by email. The approver is a single release manager who can use the AWS Management Console, and the approval history must remain in the pipeline execution record. The team does not want to introduce a separate approval tool or write code. Staging deployment results are verified by automated tests, and the approver usually responds in the console within a few hours of receiving the email. The pipeline runs once or twice a day. Which implementation has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a Lambda invoke action after the staging deployment, and implement the function so that it sends an email and then checks the approval status in Amazon DynamoDB.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disable the transition in front of the production stage and have the release manager re-enable the transition in the console when needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run a script in the AWS CodeBuild project of the staging deployment stage that waits until an approval phrase is entered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a manual approval action after the staging deployment, connect an Amazon SNS topic, and have the release manager subscribe to it by email.

explanation: A manual approval action stops the pipeline at that point and records approval or rejection, and connecting an SNS topic sets up the email notification without any code. Building the approval flow with Lambda means you operate the code and the state store yourself. Disabling a transition has no notification and no approval record, so it is hard to call it an approval procedure. A script that waits for input in the build stage does not match the purpose of CodeBuild and incurs cost while waiting.

prompt: An Amazon DynamoDB Query on a product management screen specifies a FilterExpression (status = ACTIVE) and a Limit of 50, and sometimes the response contains 0 items or only 3 items, so the screen displays that there are no active items. In reality there are hundreds of active items, and the table key design has no problem for the Query condition. The data evaluated by a single Query is limited to 1 MB, and the screen must show all active items page by page. The table has far more inactive items. Which is the MOST appropriate way to fetch all active items without omission, without greatly changing the code structure and without unnecessarily increasing the number of read requests?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raise Limit to a large maximum value so that all items that pass the filter are returned in a single Query.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on ConsistentRead for the Query to guarantee that all the latest data is read before the filter is applied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remove the FilterExpression and put the status attribute in ProjectionExpression so that the server returns only active items.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the response contains LastEvaluatedKey, pass it as ExclusiveStartKey and repeat the Query until there is no LastEvaluatedKey.

explanation: The correct answer is pagination, which passes LastEvaluatedKey as ExclusiveStartKey and repeats until there is no more LastEvaluatedKey. A Query reads up to Limit or the 1 MB page limit before applying the filter, so LastEvaluatedKey can remain even when a page has few or no matching items. Raising Limit does not remove the 1 MB limit, so pagination is still required. Strong consistency is only a freshness matter and has nothing to do with the page limit. ProjectionExpression only selects the attributes to return and does not filter items.

prompt: An AWS CodeBuild build needs a private npm registry token. It is currently put in plaintext in the project environment variables, so the value is visible in the console and in the build settings, and it was flagged in a security audit. Builds run dozens of times a day, the token is rotated once a month, and rotation is managed in AWS Secrets Manager. The team does not want to modify the build project settings every time the token changes. The CodeBuild project runs outside a VPC, and its service role is dedicated to this project. The secret is in the same account and Region and is encrypted with the default key. Which is the safest method that requires few changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep the environment variable as plaintext but add a post-processing step to the buildspec that masks the token string in build logs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reference the secret by using a secrets-manager mapping in the env section of the buildspec, and allow GetSecretValue for that secret on the CodeBuild service role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put the token in an .npmrc file, commit it to the source repository, and restrict repository access to build owners only.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upload the token file to an Amazon S3 bucket, download and use it on every build, and allow bucket access only through the service role.

explanation: The secrets-manager environment variable mapping in the buildspec fetches the secret value at build time and injects it, so the value does not remain in plaintext in the project settings, and a value rotated in Secrets Manager is automatically reflected in the next build. Keeping a plaintext environment variable and only adding masking does not solve the problem of the value remaining in the settings. Committing it to the repository leaves the secret in the history. An S3 file requires a separate rotation procedure and adds one more point to manage.

prompt: An order processing AWS Lambda function in an online store calls cloudwatch:PutMetricData synchronously on every invocation to record counts of processed items and errors. The dashboard must show order metrics in near real time and alarms must be set on them, but this synchronous call increases function latency and incurs API call costs. The team wants to produce metrics without increasing latency while also being able to find detailed logs for problem requests right away. The team does not want to operate separate collection infrastructure. The metrics are numeric values such as counts and error numbers, and one-minute granularity is sufficient. The function is written in Node.js and already outputs structured JSON logs. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Output JSON logs in EMF format so that Amazon CloudWatch extracts metrics asynchronously, and query the original logs with Logs Insights.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Move the PutMetricData call to a separate thread, but wait for the thread to finish before responding so that metrics are not lost, keeping the number of calls the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export the logs to Amazon S3, aggregate counts with Amazon Athena queries, and periodically publish the results as metrics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Record the counts in AWS X-Ray annotations, check totals on the service map, and do not create separate CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: The correct answer is to output logs in the embedded metric format (EMF). When metric definitions are placed in structured logs, CloudWatch extracts metrics from the logs asynchronously, so the function does not call the metrics API synchronously and latency does not increase, and the same log events can be queried with Logs Insights to see the cause. Moving the call to a thread does not help if the function still waits before responding, because the latency remains. Aggregation with S3 and Athena does not fit the near-real-time metric and alarm requirements. X-Ray annotations are for trace search and do not replace ordinary CloudWatch metrics and alarms.

prompt: A team has run an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment with an Amazon RDS database included in the environment, created in the console. It now wants to create a new environment with a new platform version and switch over by swapping CNAMEs (blue/green), and it plans to terminate the old environment after the switch. The database is MySQL, write traffic occurs continuously, and the existing data must be preserved during the switch. The team wants to minimize downtime. The current environment is in a single Region, and the new environment will be created in the same VPC subnets. The application reads the database endpoint as an environment property. What is the SAFEST approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Include RDS in the environment as well when creating the new environment so that it is newly created, and proceed on the assumption that swapping CNAMEs alone moves the data to the new environment's database.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Terminate the existing environment to leave the database as a snapshot, create a new environment with the same name, restore from the snapshot, and accept a short downtime.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply the Retain deletion policy to the database first, then in a separate operation decouple the database from the environment and leave it as an independent external RDS instance; then connect the new environment by directly configuring that endpoint and the security group allowance, and swap the CNAMEs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediately after the CNAME swap, change the deletion policy of the old environment's database to Delete to clean up so that the two environments do not share the same instance.

explanation: A database included in an environment is tied to the environment lifecycle and does not fit a blue/green switch. The Elastic Beanstalk documentation explains that an external (decoupled) database can be connected from multiple environments and enables blue/green deployments. The procedure is to apply the Retain deletion policy first and then apply Decouple database as a separate operation (if applied together, the new policy is ignored, and if the existing policy is Delete or Snapshot, you can lose the database), and the decoupled DB remains as an external RDS instance whose environment properties and security group must be configured directly for the connection. A CNAME swap does not move the DB, and a DB newly included in the new environment is empty. Restoring after terminating the environment causes downtime and differs from the blue/green approach. Changing the deletion policy to Delete carries a high risk of losing data.

prompt: When stream processing that forwards order events to a downstream search service gets blocked, data delay in the downstream service grows. An AWS Lambda function invoked from Amazon DynamoDB Streams keeps throwing an exception on a particular record, so processing of that shard stops and IteratorAge keeps increasing. Normal records must continue to be processed, and the location information of the failed batch must be kept so that it can be analyzed later. The function must process changes to the same item in order, and the failure records can be received in Amazon SQS or Amazon SNS. There are only one or two problem records, and the code causing the problem will be fixed in a few days. Which TWO configurations are MOST appropriate for isolating the problem without losing data? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Limit retries with MaximumRetryAttempts and specify an SQS queue as the on-failure destination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set StartingPosition to LATEST again and re-create the mapping so that only records after the current time are read.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise ParallelizationFactor to 10 so that the shard containing the problem record is processed with more concurrent invocations to increase processing speed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError on the event source mapping so that a failed batch is split in two to narrow down the problem record.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Greatly increase BatchSize to reduce the share that the problem record occupies in the whole batch in a single invocation.

explanation: The correct answers are to turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError and to set a retry limit together with an on-failure destination. Splitting the batch narrows down the range containing the problem record so that normal records can be processed first, and when the retry limit is exceeded, Lambda skips that batch and leaves batch information such as the shard ID and sequence numbers in the destination queue so that the shard does not stay blocked. The destination does not include the record body, so the records are looked up and analyzed with that information within the stream retention period. The default is -1 retry attempts (unlimited until expiry), so without setting it the processing keeps getting blocked. Increasing concurrent invocations does not help because the same record keeps failing, restarting with LATEST loses the skipped records, and increasing the batch size actually enlarges the failure range.

prompt: An AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployment is run on 10 Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances are attached to an Application Load Balancer target group, and the normal traffic can be handled by even five instances. The default OneAtATime configuration is too slow, and AllAtOnce cannot be used because of the risk of a total outage. During a deployment, at least half of the instances must handle traffic normally, and the company wants to avoid the cost of adding instances during a deployment. The deployment group automatically deregisters instances from the target group and reattaches them after the deployment, and the deployment script takes an average of 2 minutes per instance. Which deployment configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choose CodeDeployDefault.HalfAtATime to deploy to at most half of the instances at a time while the rest handle traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choose CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce and connect a rollback alarm so that the deployment is rolled back to the previous version immediately if a problem occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime and increase the number of instances in the deployment group to 20 to shorten the deployment time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Choose CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes to send 10% of the traffic to the new version first.

explanation: HalfAtATime deploys to at most half of the instances (rounded down) at a time, so it is faster than OneAtATime while always leaving at least half of the instances outside the deployment. AllAtOnce targets all instances at the same time, so there is a risk of an outage, which does not fit the conditions. Adding instances increases cost and leaves the deployment method itself unchanged, so it does not fundamentally solve the speed problem. The Lambda canary configurations are for the Lambda platform and cannot be used for EC2 in-place deployments.

prompt: In an AWS Lambda REST backend built with Java 17 and a large Spring-based codebase, initialization takes 4 to 5 seconds on cold starts, which makes p99 latency spike. A rewrite that changes frameworks is not realistic. The API invokes the function through an alias named live that points to a published version, and because of budget constraints, approaches that add charges, such as provisioned concurrency, cannot be used. The function runs on the x86_64 architecture, and deployments are done in CI by publishing a new version and moving the alias. Most of the initialization code is loading the Spring context. Which is the MOST appropriate way to reduce cold starts while keeping code structure changes to a minimum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on the live alias to secure initialized execution environments in advance and accept the resulting charges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable SnapStart on the unpublished version ($LATEST) and change the API integration target to $LATEST to apply it without any code changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise the function memory to the maximum of 10,240 MB to increase CPU for the initialization phase and leave the code as is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable SnapStart on the function version that the live alias points to, publish a new version, and have the alias point to that version.

explanation: The correct answer is to enable SnapStart for a published version and have the alias point to that version. SnapStart takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment when a version is published and restores it to reduce cold starts, and there is no additional charge for Java managed runtimes. Provisioned concurrency incurs charges and cannot be used together with SnapStart on the same version. SnapStart can be used only on published versions and aliases that point to them, so it does not work on $LATEST. Raising memory to the maximum only increases cost and leaves the initialization structure unchanged.

prompt: Someone appears to have manually changed the inbound rules of a security group created by AWS CloudFormation in the console during operation. The stack is production, and the change history remains in AWS CloudTrail, but the audit team wants a report that shows, at the property level and at a glance, the difference between the template and the current state. The check must not modify resources or update the stack, and the stack has dozens of resources of the same type. The audit team needs a result that compares the property values defined in the template with the actual property values side by side, and does not care when the last healthy state was. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a standard change set to preview the changes that would result from applying the current template as is, and find the properties that differ.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a stack update with the same template so that CloudFormation overwrites the manual changes and restores the original state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Search CloudTrail for all security group API call events and have a person trace the changes while comparing them with the template.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run stack drift detection and check the drift status of each resource and the differences between expected and actual properties.

explanation: Drift detection compares the actual configuration of the stack resources with the expected configuration defined in the template and reports the status and property differences per resource, without changing any resources. A standard change set compares only the new template with the last deployed template, so it cannot show manual changes if the template is unchanged. Updating with the same template is an attempt at remediation, not verification, and conflicts with the conditions. Searching CloudTrail requires a person to compare with the template one by one, which is inefficient for a property-level check.

prompt: An AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment runs 12 instances and is deployed to even during business hours. Average traffic is constant throughout the day, and the instance type and count do not change because of deployments. Total processing capacity must not decrease during a deployment, but the cost of launching 12 entirely new instances is a burden. Updating the existing instances in place is acceptable. During a deployment, a batch must not receive traffic until the health check of the new version is complete, and deployments happen three or four times a day. The environment has a load-balanced configuration. Which deployment policy that meets the requirements is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choose the Rolling with additional batch policy and set the batch size to 25% of the total.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choose the Rolling policy and set the batch size to 25% of the total, so that each batch is taken out of service, reattached, and waits for the health check.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Choose the Immutable policy to deploy the new version first to 12 new instances in a separate Auto Scaling group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Choose the All at once policy to update all instances at the same time and minimize deployment time.

explanation: Rolling with additional batch first launches a new batch to maintain capacity, updates in batches, and terminates the additional instances when finished, so the extra cost is limited to the size of one batch. Plain Rolling reduces capacity by the batch size while a batch is out of service. Immutable maintains capacity but launches 12 entirely new instances, which costs more. All at once causes a brief outage.

prompt: In a customer data migration job, an AWS Lambda function reads a CSV file from Amazon S3 and loads it into a provisioned-mode Amazon DynamoDB table by using BatchWriteItem (25 items at a time). All calls end with HTTP 200, but after the load finishes, about 3% of the items are missing from the table. During the load, there are periods when write capacity is intermittently exceeded, and the load is not a one-time job but repeats every week. The company does not want to increase write capacity because of budget. A single CSV file contains hundreds of thousands of items, and the average item size is about 1 KB. The code currently does not check the BatchWriteItem response. Which is the MOST appropriate way to eliminate the missing items?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Replace BatchWriteItem with TransactWriteItems to increase the number of items that can be included at once, and resend a failed transaction in its entirety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a loop that immediately calls the same request again without waiting whenever UnprocessedItems is returned, to minimize the retry interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check UnprocessedItems in the response, and if it is not empty, apply exponential backoff and resend only those items with BatchWriteItem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the Lambda function timeout and memory so that BatchWriteItem calls are processed to the end without exceeding capacity.

explanation: The correct answer is to resend only UnprocessedItems with exponential backoff. BatchWriteItem returns items it could not process, for example because capacity was exceeded, as UnprocessedItems rather than as an error, so some items can be missing even with HTTP 200, and retrying immediately repeats the same throttling, so backoff is recommended. TransactWriteItems uses double the read and write capacity per item, which conflicts with the cost constraint. Immediate repetition without waiting can make throttling worse. Timeout and memory have nothing to do with the write capacity limit on the DynamoDB side.

prompt: A payment service consists of several microservices and AWS Lambda functions, and failure analysis takes a long time. When a customer inquiry comes in, the team must quickly find only that customer's request flow. In the order service traced with AWS X-Ray, the team needs to search for only slow requests of a specific customer ID by using a filter expression, and also wants to leave an order detail JSON object in the same trace, but there is no need to search by this object. The team does not want to change the service map structure. Tracing is already turned on for Lambda and for service SDK calls, and the team can record values directly in code with the X-Ray SDK. Which is the MOST appropriate way to record the two pieces of data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Record the customer ID as an annotation and use it in the filter expression, and record the order detail object as metadata because it does not need to be searched.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Record both the customer ID and the order detail object in metadata and search by the metadata key in the filter expression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Record both the customer ID and the order detail object as annotations so that both values can be searched with filter expressions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put the customer ID in the segment name to create a separate service node for each customer, and put the detail object in the subsegment name.

explanation: The correct answer is to record the customer ID as an annotation and the order detail object as metadata. Annotations are simple key-value pairs that are indexed for use in filter expressions and GetTraceSummaries, while metadata can hold any type such as objects or lists but is not indexed and cannot be used for search. If both are put in metadata, the customer ID cannot be searched. An object cannot be put in an annotation, and there is also a per-trace limit on the number of annotations. Putting values in segment names splits the service graph into as many nodes as there are customers, making the map unreadable.

prompt: In a data collection pipeline, a nightly batch AWS Lambda function writes in bulk to Amazon DynamoDB and intermittently receives ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. A developer built a loop that catches the exception and immediately retries three times without waiting, but failures actually increased when traffic surged, and multiple Lambda instances retry at the same moment. Increasing table capacity is not possible in this cycle. Code changes are possible. The batch only needs to finish before dawn, so it is fine if it becomes somewhat slower, but writes must not be lost. The SDK currently uses its default configuration. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a fixed 100 ms wait in the retry loop so that all instances retry at the same interval, and keep the number of attempts the same.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Widen the retry targets to include client errors such as ValidationException so that any error is retried with exponential backoff, and keep the number of attempts the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off SDK retries and send failed writes immediately to an SQS DLQ so that a person manually reruns them later.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remove the custom retry loop and use the SDK's standard retry mode (exponential backoff with jitter), increasing only the maximum number of attempts if needed.

explanation: The correct answer is to remove the custom loop and use the SDK's standard retry mode. Standard mode retries throttling errors with exponential backoff and jitter, which spreads out the retry times of the instances, and the maximum number of attempts can be adjusted by configuration. A fixed wait has no jitter, so the retries still pile up at the same time. Errors in which the request itself is wrong, such as ValidationException, do not succeed even when retried, so they are not retry targets. Turning off retries and handling failures manually makes people deal with even transient throttling, which raises the operational burden.

prompt: A developer is deploying an AWS CDK app for the first time to the ap-northeast-2 Region of a newly created account. The app includes AWS Lambda code assets and a container image. cdk deploy succeeds up to synthesizing the AWS CloudFormation template but stops at the asset upload step with an error saying that this environment requires bootstrapping. The team often creates and uses new accounts and Regions, so it wants a repeatable method and wants to avoid creating resources manually. The CDK app and account credentials are properly configured on the developer's PC, and another CDK app is already deployed in us-east-1 of the same account. Which action is MOST appropriate to resolve this error?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run cdk synth again to generate a new CloudFormation template, which automatically creates the resources required for asset upload.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an S3 bucket manually and hardcode the asset path in the template so that CDK uploads without bootstrapping.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run cdk bootstrap in that account and Region to first deploy the CDKToolkit stack, which contains an S3 bucket for assets, an Amazon ECR repository, and IAM roles for deployment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upload the generated template directly in the CloudFormation console to create the stack, so that the assets are deployed without preparing the CDK environment.

explanation: CDK requires the S3 bucket and ECR repository for uploading assets, and the deployment roles, to be prepared in advance by the bootstrap stack, and this preparation is needed once for each combination of account and Region. synth only creates a template and does not create environment resources. Creating a bucket manually and hardcoding the path is a makeshift workaround that bypasses CDK's asset management, and the image asset problem remains. Even if the template is uploaded through the console, the asset files still are not uploaded anywhere.

prompt: An API's AWS Lambda function has long first-request latency from cold starts during the morning peak. The team always sends traffic through the live alias and, when deploying a new version, changes only the version the alias points to. Traffic concentrates on weekday mornings and is almost nonexistent at other times, and a new version of the function code is published about once a day and the alias is updated. The team wants to reduce the cost of initialized environments that go unused at night. The function runs outside a VPC, initialization takes about 3 seconds, and concurrent executions normally rise to about 30 at the morning peak. Which configuration is MOST appropriate for reducing cold starts while keeping this deployment flow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on the $LATEST version so that the most recently uploaded code is always on standby in an initialized state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set reserved concurrency on the function so that other functions cannot use the concurrency and execution environments are initialized in advance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the function memory to the maximum to reduce initialization time and leave the alias settings as they are so that cold starts disappear.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on the live alias and adjust the value with an Application Auto Scaling schedule to match the peak hours.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency is a feature that initializes execution environments in advance and can be configured only on a published version or an alias, so setting it on the live alias that receives traffic keeps the deployment flow, and schedule-based adjustment also manages cost. It cannot be configured on $LATEST. Reserved concurrency only guarantees capacity and sets an upper limit and does not pre-initialize. Increasing memory can make execution faster but does not eliminate cold starts themselves.

prompt: A single-page application (SPA) running at https://app.example.com reads a JSON file in an Amazon S3 bucket directly with fetch, but the browser console shows an error that the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is missing. The bucket policy already allows reading that object, and curl can retrieve it normally. Other objects in this bucket must remain private, and the security team wants the allowed scope opened only as much as necessary. The SPA only reads with GET requests from the browser and does not send credentials such as cookies, and the team does not want to build a server-side proxy. Which is the MOST appropriate way to solve the problem while keeping security and without server code?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the Principal in the bucket policy to a wildcard so that all principals can read the objects, which removes the browser's access denial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the fetch call option to no-cors mode so that the browser skips the cross-origin check and can read the response body.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on SSE-KMS default encryption on the bucket so that the browser recognizes the encrypted response as coming from an allowable origin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the bucket's CORS configuration, specify the app origin as AllowedOrigins and GET as AllowedMethods.

explanation: If curl works but only the browser is blocked, the cause is not a permissions issue but the missing CORS response header, and specifying the allowed origin and method in the bucket CORS configuration makes S3 return that header. Widening the bucket policy has nothing to do with CORS and only enlarges the access scope. no-cors mode makes the response opaque, so the JSON body cannot be read. Encryption at rest has no relationship to CORS headers.

prompt: When saving a notification configuration that invokes an AWS Lambda function on the ObjectCreated event of an Amazon S3 bucket, an error occurs saying that there is no permission to invoke the target function. The function execution role already has S3 read permission. The bucket and the function are in the same account and the same Region, the notification is used only for new object uploads, and the target function is deployed with IaC, not the console. The security team requires the principle of least privilege. The notification configuration goes from one bucket to one function only, and the account ID is injected into the template as a parameter. A bucket in another account must not be able to invoke this function. Which is the MOST appropriate way to resolve this problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add the S3 service principal to the trust policy of the Lambda execution role so that S3 assumes this role and invokes the function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the Lambda function's resource-based policy, allow the S3 principal to perform InvokeFunction with a condition on the ARN of that bucket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add an allow for lambda:InvokeFunction to the Lambda execution role so that the function can invoke itself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow s3:GetObject for the Lambda service principal in the S3 bucket policy so that the function can read objects even without an event and also stand in for the invoke permission.

explanation: Because S3 is the principal that invokes the function, the function's resource-based policy must allow the S3 service principal to make only calls that come from that bucket (SourceArn). The execution role is the role the function code uses when it calls AWS, so it has nothing to do with the trigger's caller, and changing its trust policy is not an invoke permission either. Giving InvokeFunction to the execution role also misses that the invoking principal is S3. Allowing GetObject in the bucket policy is only an object read permission and not an event invocation permission.

prompt: In an Amazon API Gateway REST API, GET /orders must be callable only by clients that have the orders/read scope, and POST /orders only by clients that have the orders/write scope. Clients receive tokens from an Amazon Cognito user pool, there are several client apps, and scope definitions are managed in a single user pool. The team does not want to operate additional server code and is not considering detailed tuning, such as whether authorization results are cached, at this time. Tokens are passed in the Authorization header on API calls, and the two methods are on the same REST API in the same stage. Which configuration enforces per-method scopes declaratively, without code, MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Define custom scopes in the user pool, specify them as per-method scopes of the Cognito authorizer, and have clients use access tokens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure the app client to issue only ID tokens, and put the scope names in the method authorization scopes so that they are checked against the claims of the ID token.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Lambda authorizer that parses the token itself and compares scope strings per path and method to return a policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue separate API keys for GET and POST, set API key required on each method, and distribute the keys to clients in place of scopes.

explanation: The Cognito user pool authorizer of API Gateway can specify OAuth scopes per method, and in that case clients must send an access token that carries the custom scopes. ID tokens are for user identity claims and are not used for scope-based authorization. A Lambda authorizer works but requires operating the code yourself, which conflicts with the declarative configuration condition. API keys are for usage control and cannot replace scope-based authorization.

prompt: A notification service receives payment completion events and sends text messages to customers, and inquiries from customers who received the same message twice are increasing. An AWS Lambda function that uses an SQS standard queue as its source sends the payment notifications. The function timeout is 60 seconds, and the queue's visibility timeout is also 60 seconds. When traffic surges, invocations are often throttled and the same batch is processed again. The notification sending API does not support idempotency. The function code can be modified, and the same message being delivered twice is explained by the at-least-once delivery characteristic of SQS standard queues. DynamoDB is already used in the account. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate to reduce duplicate sends? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the visibility timeout of the source queue to at least six times the function timeout so that messages do not become visible again even during retries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shorten the message retention period of the source queue so that messages that have remained for a long time are not delivered again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the function memory to raise CPU and reduce processing time per invocation, leaving the timeout as is and keeping the visibility timeout at its current value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the batch size to the maximum so that more messages are processed in a single invocation and the number of invocations is reduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conditionally write the processing history to DynamoDB by using the message ID as the key, and skip sending the notification for a message that has already been processed.

explanation: The correct answers are to increase the visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout and to add idempotency handling. The Lambda documentation recommends a visibility timeout of at least six times the function timeout to allow for throttling retries, and if the time is insufficient, messages that are being processed or waiting to be retried become visible again and are invoked in duplicate. The event source mapping processes at least once, so the code must be safe against duplicates. Increasing the batch size can increase the number of messages that return when one batch fails, which can make duplicates worse. The retention period is just the total time a message stays in the queue and has nothing to do with redelivery. Increasing memory to shorten processing time leaves the margin of the visibility timeout relative to the timeout unchanged, so the risk of duplicates during throttling retries remains.

prompt: The response to GET /products?category=...&page=... of a product lookup REST API barely changes for 5 minutes, but 800 requests per second are passed to the backend, putting a heavy load on the database. When stage caching was turned on, a problem appeared in which the response cached first is returned even when the category differs. It is acceptable to the business to show product data that is about 5 minutes old. The team does not want to modify the backend code. There are hundreds of combinations of category and page values in the query string, and cache capacity is sufficient. Most requests concentrate on the same popular combinations. Which method reduces backend calls the most while returning correct responses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the cache TTL to 0 seconds so that no cache entries are stored and every request is newly generated by the backend.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have clients send the Cache-Control: max-age=0 header on every request to invalidate the cache and replace it with a new response, ensuring freshness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the category and page query string parameters as cache keys and set the TTL to 300 seconds so that responses are cached separately for each parameter combination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise the stage cache capacity to the largest size, hoping that responses for different categories do not overwrite each other.

explanation: The correct answer is to specify category and page as cache key parameters and set the TTL to 300 seconds. The API Gateway cache stores responses separately for each value of the parameters included in the cache key, so a different category becomes a different entry, and for 5 minutes responses are served from the cache without calling the backend. The cause of the current problem is that the same response is returned even when parameters not in the key differ. A TTL of 0 turns the cache off. A client's max-age=0 header refills the cache only when the client has permission to invalidate, and using it on every request removes the benefit of the cache and increases the load; without permission it is rejected or ignored. Increasing capacity does not change the cache key configuration.

prompt: A mobile app and a single-page application (SPA) sign in with the Amazon Cognito hosted UI. Both apps are client apps where users sign in directly, and there is no separate backend server. Neither app can safely store a client secret, and the company also wants to avoid exposing tokens in the browser URL. The security team wants to follow the latest OAuth recommendations. Sign-in is done through the hosted UI, and the app bundles are distributed to users, so internal code can be easily viewed. The user pool and hosted UI domain are already configured. Which app client configuration is the most secure for the user sign-in flow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable the implicit grant so that tokens are received immediately in the redirect URL fragment right after authentication and used.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an app client with a client secret, include the secret in the app bundle in obfuscated form, and use the authorization code grant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable the client credentials grant so that the app calls the token endpoint with the secret and receives tokens on behalf of the user.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the authorization code grant with PKCE in a public app client that has no secret.

explanation: For public clients that cannot keep a secret, the authorization code grant with PKCE is recommended because it prevents code interception without a secret, and tokens are delivered in the token endpoint response, not in the URL. The implicit grant exposes tokens in the URL. A secret obfuscated in the bundle can still be extracted. The client credentials grant is a machine-to-machine flow, not a user sign-in flow, so it does not fit user authentication.

prompt: Microservice teams deploy independently of each other and use Amazon SNS for event fan-out. The payment team's SQS queue and the shipping team's SQS queue are subscribed to an SNS standard topic that publishes order events. The shipping team's queue must receive only events whose orderType is DELIVERY. There are millions of order events per day, so the company also wants to reduce the cost of delivering unnecessary messages, and it wants to keep changes to publisher and consumer code to a minimum. The shipping team's consumer already reads and processes messages from SQS, and the publisher can be modified to attach message attributes with the SDK. The payment team must continue to receive all events. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attach an orderType message attribute when publishing, and set a subscription filter policy on the shipping team's subscription that matches only DELIVERY.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Split the topic by order type and change the code so that the publisher determines the type and publishes only to the corresponding topic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a filtering AWS Lambda function in front of the shipping team's queue and configure it to read and then delete messages that are not DELIVERY.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Let the shipping team's queue receive all messages, and have the consumer application check orderType just before processing and skip those that do not apply.

explanation: The correct answer is to attach a message attribute and set a filter policy on the shipping team's subscription. A per-subscription filter policy makes SNS deliver only messages that match the condition to the subscriber, so unnecessary deliveries are reduced without consumer code, and the publisher only needs to add one attribute. Splitting the topic greatly changes the publisher code and configuration. A filtering Lambda function adds steps of reading and deleting after messages are put in the queue, which increases cost and operational burden. Having the consumer skip messages still incurs delivery and receipt costs and requires changing consumer code.

prompt: An internal management portal signs in through an Amazon Cognito user pool. Users in the admin group must be able to write to a specific Amazon S3 bucket, and users in the viewer group must only read. The browser calls Amazon S3 directly with the AWS SDK, and an IAM user cannot be created for each user. The portal has hundreds of users and only two groups, and the security team wants no code deployment to be required when permissions change. After signing in to the user pool, the browser receives temporary credentials from an identity pool. Administrators can directly change the permission policies of the two roles in IAM. Which configuration has the LEAST operational overhead while enforcing permissions on the server side?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create two IAM users, one per group, put each access key in the web app bundle, and have the app call S3 with the key that matches the signed-in group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give write permission to a single authenticated role of the identity pool, and implement the web app code to hide the upload button if the user is in the viewer group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Assign an IAM role to each user pool group, and configure the identity pool's authenticated role selection as Choose role from token.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create, deploy, and operate yourself a separate authentication API in which an AWS Lambda function checks the group at each sign-in, issues IAM user access keys, and returns them to the browser.

explanation: When an IAM role is assigned to a user pool group, it is carried in the cognito:roles and preferred_role claims of the ID token, and if the identity pool is configured to choose the role from the token, temporary credentials for the role that matches the group are issued, so S3 access is enforced by IAM. Putting keys in the bundle exposes long-term keys. Hiding a button is only UI and does not enforce permissions. A separate API that issues keys leaves the burden of operating it yourself and the long-term credential problem.
